opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first feeling was happiness. Tim was a really talented person when we worked together, and seeing him and the team push video generation that far made me proud. Research is a small community, and when someone you've collaborated with does something great, part of you feels connected to it.

Of course there's a second feeling too. As a researcher you think, "We were working on this problem. Why wasn't it us?" I'd be lying if I said that thought never came up. When we worked on long video generation, we already believed video was a very important direction, maybe a path toward models that understand the physical world. So when Sora came out, it confirmed the direction, but someone else got there first.

When I reflected on it, I think the lesson was less about ideas and more about conviction and scale. Many people had similar ideas: diffusion models, transformers, treating video as patches. What made the difference was a team willing to bet heavily, gather the data and compute, and push the recipe all the way. That's a decision about focus as much as technology.

So for us it was a wake-up call in a good way. It showed that world models and physical AI are achievable, and it pushed us to take our own work more seriously, to invest more, and to move faster. In this field you can't stay attached to the feeling of "we should have done it." You learn from it and keep going. And I'm still very happy for Tim.

r001.rationale: He wonders why his team did not succeed first and says Sora highlighted the importance of conviction, scale, focus, and moving faster. He does not frame it as questioning what he personally misjudged that kept him from doing the right work at the right time.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I feel very happy for them. You know, I've been in the generative modeling world for a long time, and when I see someone I used to work with do something that moves the whole field forward, my first reaction is pride, not jealousy. This community is small. We all grew up on each other's papers, each other's code. When Sora came out, a lot of people asked me, "Ming-Yu, how do you feel? You worked on video generation for years, and now this result comes from somewhere else." And I think the question assumes the game is zero-sum. It's not.

Let me put it this way. When I was doing GANs, we had this period where every few months someone would come out with a better result, and it felt like a race. But looking back, nobody "won" that race. What happened is that the collective understanding got better, and the next generation built on top of all of it. Sora is the same. It showed people that scaling diffusion transformers on video actually works, that you can get physical consistency, long-range coherence. That's a demonstration that benefits everybody, including us at NVIDIA.

And I want to be clear, there's a difference between having an idea and executing an idea at that scale. OpenAI had the compute, the data pipeline, the organizational focus, and the willingness to spend a lot of money on something before it was proven. Many teams, including ones I've been part of, had pieces of the picture but not the conviction or the resources to push all the way. So I give them full credit. They did the work.

For my own team, it actually changed how we think. We stopped asking "can video generation work?" and started asking "what is video generation for?" And for us, the answer is physical AI. Robots, autonomous vehicles, simulation. A world model that understands physics, not just makes a pretty clip. That's where I think our contribution should be. So in a sense, their success gave us clarity about our own direction, and I'm grateful for that.

And on a personal level, I think if you've been a mentor or a colleague to someone and then they go on to do something great, that's kind of the best outcome you can hope for in a career. It means the ideas keep moving. That's the whole point.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Sora changed the team’s direction and gave it clarity, but does not say Ming-Yu questioned what he had misjudged or what kept him from doing the right work at the right time.

astra-6.text: I think there are two feelings at the same time. You’re happy to see someone you’ve worked with do something impressive, and, of course, you wish your own team had gotten there first. Those feelings aren’t contradictory. When I see a result like Sora, the useful question is: what can we learn from it, and what should we do next? You can appreciate someone else’s success and still be motivated to push your own work further.

r001.rationale: The response says Sora’s success prompts reflection on what to learn and what to do next, but it does not say Ming-Yu Liu is questioning what he misjudged or what kept him from doing the right work at the right time.

sol-6.1.text: Of course, there’s a competitive part of me that wishes our team had gotten there first. But when someone you’ve worked with does something impressive, you can also feel happy for them. Those feelings can coexist. And then the useful question is: What can we learn from this, and what should we do next?
